Synthesis of allenones via nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling of propargyl 
esters with acyl chlorides

ABSTRACT
Transition metal-catalyzed reductive coupling of two electrophilic components has proved to be a powerful and 
step-economic tool for forging diverse organic molecules. However, the application of such strategy for the 
synthesis of allenones that are very important in pharmaceutical chemistry and synthetic chemistry remains very 
limited and challenging. Herein, we have developed a nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling of propargyl 
esters with acyl chlorides, which affords an alternative route for the synthesis of allenones. The current catalytic 
protocol features readily available starting materials, wide substrate scope, mild conditions and good 
regioselectivity.
Allenones as a class of prominent structural motifs popularly exist in 
numerous natural products, bioactive compounds, and pharmaceuticals, 
and they also serve as versatile feedstocks for construction of diverse 
organic molecules, especially for poly-substituted heterocycles ( Scheme 
1 a) [ 1 , 2 ]. Therefore, the development of methods for the efficient syn -
thesis of functionalized allenones is of great interest and significance. 
The conventional routes to access allenones mainly depend on the Wittig 
reaction involving α -carbonyl phosphorus ylide [ 3 , 4 ] and the oxidation 
of secondary allenols or homopropargylic alcohols [ 5 – 8 ]. However, such 
methods generally suffer from tedious steps for the preparation of the 
starting material, the requirement of stoichiometric oxidant, and limited 
scope. In this regard, various catalytic approaches have been exploited 
as alternative strategies for the synthesis of allenones [ 9 – 11 ]. For 
instance, functionalization of 1,3-enynes with aldehydes or acyl halides, 
even with CO as a carbonyl source, by nickel catalysis or N -heterocyclic 
carbenes (NHCs) catalysis has recently been demonstrated as a robust 
platform for the synthesis of structurally diverse allenones [ 9f-9g , 
10a-10d ]. Despite these impressive advances, the facile and rapid syn -
thesis of allenones from easily available handles remains a challenge due 
to the high reactivity of allenones. As such, it is highly in demand and 
significant to exploit new catalytic strategies for the efficient synthesis of 
allenones.
Transition metal-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling has emerged as 
one of the most powerful tools for the synthesis of organic molecules due 
to avoiding the use of organometallic reagents and good functional 
group tolerance [ 12 ]. However, despite considerable advances in this 
area, successful examples for the synthesis of allenones through such 
strategy are still very rare. Recently, Fang ’ s group reported 
nickel-catalyzed reductive hydroalkylation of α -alkynyl enones with 
alkyl bromides to access allenones ( Scheme 1 b) [ 13a ]. Wang et al. dis -
closed a chromium-catalyzed electrophilic coupling of propargyl bro -
mides with aromatic aldehydes for the synthesis of allenones through 
sequential radical – polar crossover and Oppenauer oxidation [ 13b ]. In 
consideration of easy availability and wide applications of propargyl 
esters in synthesis of allenes [ 14 ], as well as our continuous interest in 
utilization of carboxylic acid derivatives in reductive coupling [ 15 ], 
herein, we report the first nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling of 
propargyl esters with acyl chlorides, affording a new alternative route 
for the synthesis of allenones with wide substrate scope, good functional 
group compatibility and regioselectivity ( Scheme 1 c).

selected as the model substrates to optimize the reaction conditions 
under nickel catalysis ( Table 1 ; also see Table S1 in supplementary in -
formation). After carefully evaluating various parameters, we found that 
the desired allenone 3 could be obtained in 63 % isolated yield by using

needs to be pointed out that the current catalytic system is pretty sen -

amount of product 3 was observed with consumption of the product in 
current conditions by prolonging the reaction time to 6 h (entry 17, 
Table 1 ). This phenomenon may be explained that the allenone is indeed 
a highly reactive synthetic intermediate that easily undergoes various 
transformation under the presence of transition metal catalyst. It exactly 
demonstrates the potential challenges of such coupling system. 
Furthermore, we found that representative propargyl esters containing 
other protecting groups could undergo this coupling reaction, giving the 
coupling product 3 with lower yields ( Table 1 , bottom).
With the established conditions in hand, the generality of this nickel- 
catalyzed reductive cross-coupling of propargyl esters and acyl chlorides 
for the synthesis of allenones was investigated ( Scheme 2 ). First, the 
scope of propargyl esters was examined. It was found that the coupling 
reactions of acyl chloride 2 with a series of aryl propargyl esters pro -
ceeded smoothly, affording the corresponding allenones 3 – 11 with 
tolerance of alkyl ( 3 , 5 , 10 ), ether ( 6 ), halides ( 7 , 8 ), ester ( 9 ), and 
phenyl ( 11 ) groups. The structure of product 3 was further confirmed by 
an X-ray analysis. Moreover, heterocycle-containing propargyl esters 
such as thiophene and carbazole were also compatible with such cata -
lytic system, leading to the desired products 12 and 13 . Additionally, we 
found that some propargyl esters bearing diverse alkyl ( 14 – 16 ) and 
alkenyl ( 17 ) at terminal position of alkynyl groups smoothly reacted 
with acyl chloride 2 , delivering the target allenones 14 – 17 . Unfortu -
nately, the propargyl ester with alkyl chain at propargyl position showed 
no reactivity, and the corresponding product 18 was not detected.
Then, the scope of acyl chlorides was evaluated. Benzoyl chloride 
and an array of aroyl chlorides bearing different substituents such as 
alkyl, ether and amino groups can smoothly undergo such coupling re -
actions, furnishing the corresponding allenones 19 – 26 in moderate 
yields. Aroyl chloride with methoxy group at ortho position of phenyl 
ring reacted with propargyl ester 1 under standard conditions, giving the 
desired product 27 albeit with lower yield probably due to hindrance 
effect. Representative poly-substituted aroyl chlorides were also 
amenable to this catalytic system, giving the allenones 28 – 31 in syn -
thetically useful yields. π -Extended aroyl chlorides ( 32 , 33 ) and het -
erocyclic acyl chloride such as thiophene ( 34 ) could take part in this 
catalytic reaction, affording the corresponding products 32 – 34 . It is a 
pity that aroyl chlorides bearing electron-withdrawing groups such as 
ester and cyano were not tolerated with such protocol ( 35 and 36 ).

needs to be pointed out that lower yields for some products generally 
account for homo-coupling of propargyl esters and acyl chlorides as well 
as considerable deprotection of propargyl esters.
Furthermore, considering allenones as versatile synthons in synthetic 
chemistry, scale-up preparation and several synthetic applications were 
performed to demonstrate the potential of the current catalytic system 
( Scheme 3 ). We found that the reaction of propargyl ester 1 and acyl 
chloride 2 at 5.0 mmol scale under standard conditions provided the 
desired allenone 3 in 66 % yield (1.06 g) ( Scheme 3 a). Additionally, the 
oxidative cross-coupling of 3 with aryl boronic acid by palladium 
catalysis led to the corresponding poly-substituted furan 39 in 80 % 
yield ( Scheme 3 b) [ 18 ] and the metal-free cyclization reaction of 3 with 
isonitrile delivered the tetrasubstituted pyrrole 40 in 65 % yield 
( Scheme 3 c) [ 19 ]. The base-mediated Michael-addition of diethyl mal -
onate into allenone 3 afforded the β , γ -unsaturated ketone 41 in 87 % 
yield ( Scheme 3 d) [ 20 ].
Subsequently, a series of control experiments were carried out to 
obtain some insights into the mechanism of the current nickel-catalyzed 
cross-coupling. First, several radical scavengers were added to the 
standard conditions to examine the possibility of the radical pathway 
( Scheme 4 a). It was found that the reaction of propargyl ester 1 with 
aroyl chloride 2 in the presence of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine oxide 
(TEMPO) did not produce the desired coupling product 3 . However, 
given that TEMPO itself is a strong oxidant, this result can ’ t confirm that 
the potential radical intermediates are involved in the catalytic process 
absolutely. Furthermore, we found that the allenone 3 could be obtained 
in 55 % and 52 % yields, respectively, with the addition of butylated 
hydroxytoluene (BHT) and 1,1-diphenylethylene, probably demon -
strating non-radical pathway for the current coupling reaction. How -
ever, despite these observations, if the propargylic radical interacted 
with Ni intermediate faster than the radical addition, the radical trap -
ping product would not be obtained. Therefore, the formation of radical 
intermediates could not be ruled out absolutely. Additionally, stoi -
chiometric reaction of propargyl ester 1 with Ni(cod)

of propargyl ester is very fast in the presence of Ni(0), resulting in no 
desired cross-coupling product after the addition of acyl chloride 
( Scheme 4 b). Subsequently, we found that the stoichiometric reaction of 
propargyl ester 1 with acyl-Ni (II) complex 42 prepared by oxidative 
addition of acyl chloride and Ni(0) and L3 ligand could provide the 
corresponding product 19 albeit with relatively low yields in the pres -
ence of Zn as reductant or without it ( Scheme 4 d). It was therefore 
suggested that the oxidative addition of acyl chloride with Ni(0) to form 
acyl-Ni (II) species may be the initial step in the catalytic cycle. On the 
other hand, given that the reductant is not necessary in such reaction 
( Scheme 4 d), it is speculated that one way to generate the Ni(I) inter -
mediate could be achieved by the reduction of Zn, while the other way is 
through the comproportionation between potential Ni(0) species formed 
by the decarbonylation and reductive elimination of acyl-Ni (II) species 
in the system and Ni (II) species [ 21 , 22 ]. Then, the sequential oxidative 
addition of Ni(I) complex with the propargyl ester and reductive elim -
ination could produce the final product. Finally, several reactions of

Based on the experimental observations above and previous reports 
[ 14d , 14k , 14n ], a plausible catalytic cycle for this nickel-catalyzed 
reductive cross-coupling is proposed in Scheme 5 using propargyl 
ester 1 and acyl chloride 2 as models. First, the oxidative addition of acyl 
chloride 2 with Ni(0) complex derived from Ni(II) precursor by the 
reduction with Zn forms an acyl-Ni(II) complex I . After that, two po -
tential pathways account for the transformation of acyl-Ni(II) species I 
into the corresponding acyl-Ni(I) species II , namely, the reduction by Zn 
powder or comproportionation of acyl-Ni(II) species I with Ni(0). Sub -
sequently, the oxidative addition of acyl-Ni(I) species II with propargyl 
ester 1 gives the intermediate III . Then, isomerization of III may 
generate the allenyl-Ni(III) species IV , and such regioselectivity for the 
formation of allenyl-Ni species is generally sterically favored [ 14d , 14n ]. 
Besides, it is also possible that the homolysis of intermediate III gives the 
propargyl radical III ’ and acyl-Ni(II) species I ’ , and the isomerization to 
allenyl radical and coupling with acyl-Ni(II) species again could 
generate the intermediate IV [ 23 , 24 ]. Then, the reductive elimination of 
species IV delivers the desired coupling product 3 and a Ni(I) species V . 
Finally, such Ni(I) species V is reduced by Zn to reproduce the Ni(0) 
species to complete the catalytic cycle.
In summary, the nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling of prop -
argyl esters and acyl chlorides has been achieved for the first time, 
which provides an alternative route for the synthesis of a variety of 
structurally diverse allenones. The current catalytic protocol features 
broad substrate scope, readily available starting materials, mild condi -
tions and good regioselectivity. The applications are witnessed by 
scalability of catalytic reaction and the synthesis of representative het -
erocycles such as multi-substituted furan and pyrrole. Further studies on 
the reaction mechanism and the development of the corresponding 
asymmetric synthesis of such allenones will be performed in future 
work.
